source.title: Feature Hedging: Correlated Features Break Narrow Sparse Autoencoders
source.authors: David Chanin; Tomás Dulka; Adrià Garriga-Alonso

page_placements.theme: SAE latents become polysemantic through absorption, hedging and co-occurrence

record.file_problem: None; the full paper text, including appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: The study refines the account of polysemantic mixtures: in its toy models, narrow SAE latents mix correlated features, but narrowness alone does not produce hedging for independent features. It also measures how hedging changes with SAE width and type.
record.gate_note: The paper measures mixtures in SAE latents, not polysemanticity of the original LLM neurons. It reports no direct test of InceptionV1 neurons, language-model MLP neuron polysemanticity, or the proposed pose/shared-feature explanation. Results cited from other papers were not recorded as rows. Balance-matryoshka benchmark metrics that do not directly measure hedging were not treated as hedging rows.
record.test_reason: The paper takes polysemantic LLM activations as its premise and studies a failure mode of sparse autoencoders trained to undo it. Every result measures mixing in SAE latents, a dictionary trained on activations. It never measures neurons of the classifier or language model. No version names SAE latents, so the study tests none of them. Its results are recorded under fits_no_version.
record.authors_conclusion: The paraphrase is broadly right. The authors attribute hedging to MSE reconstruction loss and say it needs only feature correlation plus an SAE narrower than the feature set. They say matryoshka SAEs trade absorption for hedging, and that SAE width is not a neutral hyperparameter. Balanced matryoshka SAEs improve most benchmarks, but absorption and hedging are not fully solved.
record.recipe_differences: The study trains sparse autoencoders on synthetic activations and LLM activations, then measures mixtures through feature-direction cosines and a decoder-change projection metric. It does not reproduce the original neuron-visualization or neuron-ablation methods.
record.method_sensitivity: Hedging varies with SAE width, feature correlation, SAE type (BatchTopK versus L1), and, more modestly, BatchTopK L0.

fits_no_version.finding: In toy models, SAEs narrower than the number of true features mix correlated or hierarchical features into one latent, with the sign following the correlation (r2, r3, r5, r8-r14). With independent features, or at full width, they learn correct features (r1, r4, r6, r7, r15, r16).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: SAE latents become polysemantic (feature hedging) when the dictionary is narrower than the true features and those features are correlated; capacity shortage alone does not cause mixing.

fits_no_version.finding: In Gemma-2-2b and Llama-3.2-1b SAEs, hedging degree falls steeply with width but stays nonzero at 65536. It is higher for BatchTopK than L1, is minor with respect to L0, and shows little layer effect (Fig 8b, unrecorded).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Hedging in LLM SAEs decreases with SAE width and depends modestly on SAE type, but not strongly on layer.

record.problems: The paper studies SAE latents rather than original model neurons. The LLM hedging measure is indirect and depends on adding latents and continued training; its number of added latents is a hyperparameter. The LLM experiments cover models up to 2b parameters and SAE widths up to 65536, which the authors attribute to compute constraints. Several plotted results are reported without exact numerical values.
record.rows_left_out: Omitted detailed balance-matryoshka benchmark outcomes in Figure 10 and Appendix Figure 18 because those reported evaluation metrics do not directly measure hedging. Also omitted the case-study example activations in Appendix A.5 because they illustrate a particular SAE latent rather than giving a separately reported quantitative hedging result.

untested.parts: No measurement of the share of polysemantic MLP neurons in language models, or how it varies by layer.
No test of whether network neurons are polysemantic because of superposition; only SAE latents are studied.
No study of polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization or noise when capacity suffices.
No variation of the network's activation function or architecture; no neuron polysemanticity rates.
No re-examination of canonical polysemantic neurons.
No study of how activation range or scoring choices change neuron polysemanticity labels.

missing.what: Hedging degree vs layer: the text says layer has no massive effect on hedging degree.
missing.versions: none (SAE latents); relevant to the fits_no_version finding

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked rows to V3 and V5, but every row measures SAE latents, which the paper itself calls 'hidden neurons of the SAE'. These are not neurons of the studied networks. The correlation-dependence result is conceptually relevant to superposition accounts, but no version covers SAE dictionaries. The reader's labels are therefore withdrawn.

versions.untested_parts: Polysemanticity of transformer MLP neurons across tokens, contexts, or layers.

The paper tests SAE latents, not whether superposition causes polysemanticity in the original network neurons. Its results concern a toy setting and SAE width/correlation, not a general account of all model polysemanticity.
Polysemanticity arising from initialization, regularization, or training noise when capacity is sufficient.

The paper varies SAE width and compares L1 and BatchTopK SAEs; it does not test SoLU, modern convnets, original-network neuron polysemanticity, or directly establish a general performance-cost tradeoff for lowering neuron polysemanticity.
Whether canonical mixed neurons detect a shared feature or related offshoots, and how often truly unrelated mixtures occur.
Whether neuron polysemanticity depends on activation range or explanation-scoring choices.

rows.subject: Toy model with 4 independent features
rows.operation_detail: Trained SAEs on synthetic activations with independent feature firings.
rows.measure: Cosine similarity of SAE encoder and decoder directions to true features; whether latents mix features
rows.value: The SAE learned correct features; no hedging was observed.
rows.note: The authors report correct features for both the 3-latent and 4-latent SAEs, despite the 3-latent SAE having fewer latents than true features.
rows.check: Measures SAE latents on synthetic data, not network neurons; bears on no version. State as a description of hedging is correct.

relation.reason: The paper takes polysemantic and superposed activations as a premise and studies SAE failure. It does not test any neuron claim. The reader's 'tests' does not fit.

tranche.reason: No version is tested. All results measure SAE latents (toy SAEs on orthogonal synthetic features and LLM SAEs), not neurons of the trained network, so T3 (a result on the claim) does not fit. The paper takes polysemantic LLM activations as the premise for SAEs and reports SAE failure modes and its own balanced matryoshka SAE, which fits T4.

source_check.notes: All six rows match the text. Values are qualitative and Fig 8 values appear only in plots. The Fig 8 caption says Gemma layer 12, but the legends also show Llama series (layer 7 per Appendix A.3). The rows concern SAE latents, not network neurons, so they are correctly unlinked from all versions.

statements.correction: Optional softening: the paper says BatchTopK SAEs appear to have more hedging than L1 SAEs. In Fig 8b the two types merge near the last layers.
statements.problem: Matches Section 4.1 and Fig 8a: steep drop with width, and no SAE reaches 0 at 65536. Minor: the text hedges the BatchTopK-vs-L1 gap ('appears') and gives no significance test.
